title: Block-GTQ: RoPE-Aware Bit Allocation for KV-Cache Quantization
hook: Most KV-cache quantizers spend bits evenly across a key. Block-GTQ shows that under RoPE some frequency blocks matter far more — and gives them more bits, hitting near-fp16 quality at 2–3 bits.
key_points: Under RoPE, a key's contribution to a future attention score splits into a position-dependent sum over 2D frequency blocks — so not all parts of a key are equally important.
Block-GTQ reframes key-cache quantization as block-wise bit allocation: high-energy RoPE blocks get more bits.
It scores each block with a label-free energy metric and greedily assigns bit widths by marginal gain.
Cuts per-layer error 32–80% at 2–3 bits/dim and wins all 367/367 layer comparisons vs uniform quantization.
Enables ~3.24x KV-cache compression with near-fp16 quality and lower memory at long context.
content_html: Quantizing the KV cache is one of the biggest levers for serving long-context LLMs cheaply. Most methods treat each cached key as a flat vector and spend bits uniformly. Block-GTQ points out that's wasteful once you account for how RoPE actually works.
extra_html:
The insight

With rotary position embeddings (RoPE), a key's contribution to a future attention logit isn't uniform — it decomposes into a position-dependent sum over two-dimensional frequency blocks. Some blocks carry far more energy than others, so quantization error in a high-energy block hurts much more. That reframes key-cache quantization as a bit-allocation problem: give sensitive blocks more bits and starve the rest.

The method and results

For each layer and KV head, Block-GTQ computes a label-free energy score per RoPE block and greedily assigns integer bit widths by marginal gain. Against uniform baselines under matched bit budgets, it cuts per-layer error by 32–80% at 2–3 bits/dim and wins all 367/367 layer comparisons. Downstream, it lifts long-context retrieval and reasoning scores sharply and supports a packed-cache serving path — the authors report roughly 3.24x KV-cache compression with near-fp16 quality, faster attention, and far lower peak memory at 128K context and beyond. Code is linked from the paper.

related.hook: Long reasoning chains blow up the KV cache. Squeeze it to 2 bits and errors snowball over thousands of decode steps — unless you fix the token scales first.

related.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization
related.hook: Already trained a giant LLM? GPTQ squeezes its weights down to 3–4 bits afterward — no retraining — with surprisingly little quality loss.

related.title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
related.hook: Not all weights are equal - protect the 1% that matter most (flagged by activation magnitude) and quantize the rest to 4-bit with minimal quality loss.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Block-GTQ argue that KV-cache keys shouldn't be quantized with uniform bit widths?
flashcards.back_html: Under RoPE, a key's contribution to attention logits decomposes into a position-dependent sum over 2D frequency blocks — high-energy blocks are more sensitive to quantization error and deserve more bits.

flashcards.prompt: How does Block-GTQ decide where to spend bits?

choices.text: Compute a label-free energy score per RoPE block, then greedily allocate bit widths by marginal gain
Give every dimension the same number of bits
Use a learned network trained on labeled data to pick bit widths

flashcards.explanation_html: For each layer and KV head it scores each RoPE frequency block's energy (no labels needed) and greedily allocates integer bit widths where they help most.
